analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in Vaughan and others against Vermillion Corporation, number 1819. Mr. Hill, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. T. Justice, may it please the court. This matter involves a system of artificial canals in extreme southern Louisiana. Their construction was begun in 1942, and it continues to this moment. They are generally 60 feet wide by 8 feet in depth, and run from the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway on the north to the Gulf of Mexico on the south, and cover an area approximately 15 to 20 miles wide from east to west. They are affected by tidal action. They connect, among other waterways, with the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, with the freshwater Bayou Canal, with the Gulf of Mexico, with Vermillion Bay on the east, and with Oyster Bayou and in the west. They are, we believe, navigable in fact, and to satisfy all tests of navigability, heretofore put forth by this court. Court. It was, I believe, most of those facts, with the exception of connection to the Gulf, that I've just recited, are undisputed between the parties. It was, however, the subject of vehement dispute in the court below as to whether or not the actual building of these canals, in fact, impaired and in some cases destroyed the navigability of pre-existing natural canals in the area. Since the case was disposed of in the trial court on summary judgment, there was no opportunity for the making of much of a record on that point. Nevertheless, the petitioners submitted an affidavit in opposition to the motion for summary judgment that said, for example, that the old freshwater bayou, which coursed from Pecan Island, Louisiana, a small municipality on a little stretch of terra firma in the middle of marshland, the old freshwater bayou coursed from there to the Gulf of Mexico and was used, among other things, to transport the United States mail. And... Council, if these maps are to be of any utility, it would be helpful if you'd indicate physically at the appropriate time, whenever you wish, what areas we're talking about. The map, if you're honest, please, was offered by the Vermilion Corporation with our consent. The only generally, or general deficiency of the map is that it does not, so far as I know, show absolutely the entirety of the canal system. The bottom of the photograph, of course, is the Gulf of Mexico. The most prominent... Where generally is the land area that we're talking about? Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honor. The most prominent waterway coursing northerly from the Gulf is on the east or right side of the photograph, and that is freshwater bayou. The most prominent entrance of the artificial system into freshwater bayou is shown approximately six inches up in the photograph from the Gulf and entering into the most prominent north-south waterway. You will see at least three artificial canals. They are absolutely straight, approximately six inches to the left of the freshwater bayou canal, which enter into the Gulf of Mexico. What you cannot see in the north is the Gulf Intracoastal waterway. What is the difference between the canal and the bayou? Being from south Louisiana and being from somewhere else, a bayou is a small... It's a bayou that's 20 or 30 feet deep. A bayou is, generally speaking, a small, fairly slow-moving body of water, which, according to its depth, might well be called a river in other places. Generally speaking, however, the term bayou refers to that which is natural. I've never heard an artificial body of water referred to by that term in Louisiana or anywhere else in my mouth. The canal is not natural, right? The freshwater bayou canal is not... The bayou canal? Now, the freshwater bayou canal is a canal which was built from 1964 to 1968, generally but not entirely, over the course of the old freshwater bayou. When I refer to freshwater bayou, I'm referring to the old natural body of water. The freshwater bayou canal, on the other hand, is not an entirely natural body of water and is not directly involved in this case. How deep are these bayou canals? Well, the artificial canals, which are the subject of this lawsuit, are generally 8 feet deep. They are somewhat shallower at points, but virtually the entirety of the system is generally 8 feet deep by 60 feet wide. Now... And generally speaking, the basic difference between a bayou and a canal is that a bayou is natural and a canal is man-made, isn't it? That's correct. That's correct. Plaintiffs were sued. Plaintiffs are residents of Pecan Island, Louisiana, and, among other things, are alleged to have supplemented their incomes by shrinking in, among other places, the artificial canals prepared by the respondents. The plaintiffs were sued under the Louisiana State Trespass Law by Vermilion Corporation for, among other things, an injunction. The plaintiffs have defended by saying in the trial court that these waters, the waters of the artificial canal system, were impressed with a navigation servitude and were navigable waters of the United States, and thus that there could be no private appropriation by injunction or otherwise, to keep citizens of the United States from being able to navigate the same. Secondly, petitioners defended in the trial court by saying that the mere filing of a lawsuit and the attempted maintenance of an injunction against public exercise of the navigation servitude was ipso facto and obstruction under the rivers and harbors act and was prohibited. Petitioners finally say in this court that the Louisiana Organic Act, which states generally that the navigable waters leading into the Gulf of Mexico shall be forever free to the citizens, also applies and prohibits the doing of that which Vermilion Corporation was allowed to do by the Louisiana State Court System. The position of the Louisiana courts is, as I read it, quite simple. The Louisiana courts found that these artificial canals were navigable, in fact, that they connected to various interstate marine highways of commerce, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, and that they did support and were capable of supporting various kinds of commerce themselves. Nevertheless, it was the position of the Louisiana court system that a canal system built on private property with private funds is a private thing, period. The questions which we believe are raised by this proceeding on. Does the navigation servitude in favor of members of the public automatically arise and exist on navigable waters of the United States? Secondly, and perhaps of somewhat less importance, but nevertheless, before this court, are the questions involving the Rivers and Harbors Act and the Louisiana Organic Act. Do they apply to preclude the respondents' essential appropriation of these canals to private use? Finally, the question is, is an artificial canal built with private funds on private lands, but which is navigable, in fact, and connected to other interstate highways of commerce, and which in its building destroyed pre-existing natural navigable canals, a navigable water of the United States impressed with a navigation servitude? I believe that you say that last issue is, you know, the facts underlying the premise are in dispute. Very much. You told us that earlier. Yes, sir. So how can we decide that question? The point of law was simply rejected by the Louisiana court system. My mind is that even assuming that they had. Yes, sir. I believe the decision of the Louisiana court of appeal, Third Circuit, is pointed in that regard, that it simply would make no difference whether I prove that or not. Well, if we rejected your first point and then came to your last point, rejected your first two, came to your last, we would have to remand to the Louisiana court. I believe so. And even if we agree with you? I believe so. If we agreed with them, we'd just discern them, right? If you agreed with the Louisiana court system in its entirety, yes, sir, but Mr. Justice... In order to remand, we'd have to disagree with them on the last point. Yes, sir. That's right. Or at least we would have to agree that the question which they said was factual, a factual question was immaterial, was material, and it would have to be found one way or the other by a prior fact. Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Yes, sir. On that point, as I understand your theory, is that if they interfered with, say, if they built a new canal X and that had an impact on an old canal Y, that was her, you're saying that's the factual issue of it. Do you have an interest in the navigation on canal Y? I'm wondering if you have any standing to complain about what they may have done to that other canal. As a bio. I'm sorry. I guess it was a bio. As a member of the public, as a citizen of the United States, in whose favor the navigation servitude on Navajo waters the United States runs, It isn't the question about shrimping in the area that's been built rather than navigating in the area that may have been impaired. But if the pre-existing natural navigable waterway had impressed on it a navigation servitude and they appropriate that servitude via destruction of that waterway, it is our position that equitably the navigation servitude must be transposed onto the new system. And I believe there is authority for that in this court in Philadelphia Company v. Stimson. I see. You've got a substitute. This is a substitute for the old urine title for that. Philadelphia Company v. Stimson is 223 U.S. 605. Mr. Hill, your first two points, at least, depend entirely upon the fact that this is water, doesn't it? Yes, sir. In other words, your argument would in no way assert that if I owned land two miles from an interstate highway and built a two-mile driveway from my property to the interstate highway, that that driveway belonged to the public, or at least that the public had open and free access to it. Would you? I would not at all, sir. So it depends entirely upon the fact these are water. What was it? Because, except for the fact that these are water, this case is very much like my hypothetical case, isn't it? Yes. In order for waterways to have any reason to be and to have any usefulness, they have to be, as they were in this case, they have to literally be born out of the public's water. They have to be tied to other interstate highways of commerce as they were in this case. They must have the public's water to exist. They, in their existence, may well affect the navigable integrity and capacity of other public waterways. None of that is true in the case of Roach. Would you have to give us an affidavit that this had always been on to the public? That is an ancillary disputed issue. You're quite correct about that, Mr. Justice Marshall. But you didn't get any more than that. That is disputed. My point, and in one of my earlier briefs, I don't know if it's in my brief to this court, that is a little bit of an interesting sidelight. My point is that Louisianians, for example, have gone on their merry way for years with people in my client's positions, in the petitioner's positions, thinking it was, generally speaking, fine for them to navigate these canals or those like them, whereas people in the position of the respondents and others similarly situated have thought that they had an absolute right to keep them out. I don't, this case has never, to my knowledge, been presented in a federal context. The only jurisprudential dealings in it have been under the Louisiana state law. It could be that the public was only there by something. That is their contention. We, of course, be able to dispute that. The congressional power to regulate is thought to be an important issue of this case as to whether or not the standard for determination of navigable waters of the United States in regulation cases under the Commerce Clause is the same as the standard for navigation servitude cases. Or whether or not the admiralty jurisdiction is applicable. I would concede... Or a variety of other applications. I would concede as primarily an admiralty lawyer that that does present a different question for, I think, a large number of reasons. I do not, however, feel that the argument has merit when only congressional power to regulate under the Commerce Clause as applied to waterways, on the one hand, and the navigation servitude on the other, are concerned. Do you think navigable waters of the United States means navigable waters belonging to the United States or navigable waters located anywhere in the United States? Navigable waters of the United States, as Ms. Oberle said this morning, belong to no one. What do you think the phrase means was my question. Navigable... It means two things. Number one, it means navigable waters, waterways which are navigable, in fact, either in their natural or ordinary condition or... Located anywhere in the United States? Located anywhere in the United States. No, certainly it doesn't mean that if it's entirely within a single state. No, if it is located entirely within a single state and connects to other bodies of water that lead to interstate waters than it is of the United States, that it is in interstate commerce. The phrase of the United States, I take to mean waters that burden or affect or have something to do with interstate commerce. I'm sorry I didn't follow the thrust of your question, but certainly I would agree with that. The fact is, as we see it, that the navigation servitude and the congressional power to regulate waterways are in one sense coterminous or are identical. Until really a very few years ago, congressional regulation of waterways, to my knowledge, had, if not exclusively, at least predominantly one object, and that was the protection of a public right to navigate. Other reasons for the exercise of congressional regulatory power as applied to waterways, for example, pollution control, are really fairly recent considerations. From the time of Gibbons v. Ogden, as I appreciate the law, the navigation servitude and the congressional power to regulate waterways have been treated as part and parcel of the same thing. If they have, and if that is correct, then we feel that the respondent's argument that there is a difference and that a different standard should be applied simply has no merit. And if it has no merit, Appalachian Electric Power v. United States would seem to us here to apply. Appalachian Electric Power says that waterways which may be rendered navigable with reasonable improvement are navigable waters of the United States. We submit that there is no difference practically and factually between digging a canal off of the intracoastal waterway or digging a canal that connects with the Gulf and, on the other hand, artificial improvement of the new river which in its natural state was no good for any sort of navigation whatsoever. They both require exactly the same sort of acts and expenditure of money and doing of work and the, generally speaking, same sorts of human activity as are required here. And the result is the same. A new body of water over which interstate commerce may be transacted. If your honors have no further questions I would like to reserve and balance my time. Very well. Mr. McCall. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, if I may go back a moment and refer to this aerial photograph. This photograph is not part of the record. It is purely an aid to assist your honors in seeing what it is we're talking about. But there's no disagreement about it. There's no disagreement about it except that I would like to point out several things with respect to it. We were told, Mr. McCall, that it was offered in evidence. I gather that it was not received in evidence. It was not offered in evidence as I understand it, your honor. I think that was a mistake. No, I'm not saying what you told us, but what your brother told us. He said it was offered in evidence. I don't think he meant that because it was not offered in evidence. He didn't mean to try it, but he did say it. It is purely, as I say, an aid for oral argument. And so that your honors will know what it is we're talking about, I am informed that the dimensions of this are approximately 10 miles to a side. And the principal aspect of this to which we would respectfully invite the court's attention is the number of canals which dead end. And that is explained by the fact that the great majority of these canals were dredged for the purpose of mineral development. The nature of the land here, which, as you can see, is on the Gulf Coast and is swamp land, is such that it is not possible to get a drilling rig in other than by floating it in. And this explains the shape of these canals and the fact that they all terminate at some point. The only canal which was dredged by the engineers is, as Council has pointed out, that canal which extends on the right-hand side of the photograph in pretty much a straight line and has taken the place that's known as Freshwater Bayou Canal. And it, to a large extent, takes the place of former Freshwater Canal. For purposes of this case, Mr. McCall, would it make any difference whether the canals were dredged for oil rigs or steamboats? Not in the least, Your Honor. Not in the least. Except to this extent, as long as it is understood that the dredging of these canals was accomplished for private purposes for use of the land. In no sense, with the exception of the Freshwater Bayou Canal, which I have mentioned, were they dredged for general use. They are there either to gain access to oil well locations, to trap lines, to access to hunting leases and places like that. But other than that, Your Honor is quite right. It makes no difference. With all respect to the canal that was dredged to replace a pre-existing bayou, you don't challenge their right to use that canal? No, sir. That's a public canal. Yeah. That was dredged by the Corps of Engineers in pursuant to a servitude which we gave them for that purpose. But that canal is not at issue in this case. What does that canal call? That canal goes from the Gulf of Mexico, which shows at the bottom of the map, to Vermilion Bay, which is up to the right and off the map or off the photograph. Vermilion Bay is part of the ocean? It's a bay from the Gulf of Mexico and to that extent it is part of the ocean. Yes, sir. If private funds had dredged that canal, suppose the canal had never reached Vermilion Bay but private funds dredged it and extended it to Vermilion Bay, would you be making the same argument about that canal? We would be making, do you mean the same argument we're presently making about that canal or about that We would contend, Your Honor, that we were entitled to keep the public out of that canal. I qualify that. What about, would Congress have the power to require you to let the public in, say for a price? Oh, I have no question about that. I think Congress' power is paramount. If it can show a public purpose, it can appropriate just about anything it wants, provided it pays for it. Would they have to pay you for it? In our opinion, they would, Your Honor. So you would say that Congress could not pass a statute that required you to let the public into this canal system that is presently at issue? That's precisely our position, Your Honor. Mr. McCall, what about the factual dispute referred to by the Louisiana Court of Appeals on page A10 of the petition where they say that the defendants contend there is a factual dispute and the factual dispute is that artificial waterways destroyed the navigability of surrounding natural waterways. Now, the Court of Appeals I understood said Louisiana law does not make that factual dispute material in a legal sense, but there is that factual dispute between you and your opponents, is there not? We do not concede, Your Honor, that there does exist such a factual dispute. The basis of that dispute is the affidavit which appears at page 54 of the RAC, 54A of the appendix. And if Your Honors will examine that affidavit carefully, bearing in mind that affidavits are not drafted by the affidavits, but by counsel, you will observe that that affidavit does not create an issue of fact. Look particularly at the last paragraph of this affidavit. If you will examine the last paragraph of that affidavit, it begins, Prior to the development of the Humboldt Canal system, deponents are aware that various portions of the natural navigable waterway, et cetera. The law of Louisiana is quite clear. When you're opposing a motion for summary judgment, you must make an affidavit that fairly meets the affidavits or the representations made by the moving party, and it must be made on personal knowledge. But that isn't the answer that the Louisiana Court of Appeals gave. They treated as I read their opinion as a permissible affidavit and simply said legally it was insufficient. Well, may I come to that? And I think I should, since Your Honor has asked the question. The answer which the Court of Appeals gave in Louisiana is to be found in an earlier decision by the courts of Louisiana, the Supreme Court of Louisiana, which is cited, I believe, in both briefs, in Ilheny v. Boussard. That was a case involving another situation wherein access was sought to private canal. And what the court held there was that even though it were established that there had been destruction of or impediment to the use of an existing canal, that would not of itself give the public the right to use the canals which had affected that destruction or substitution. And the reasoning for that was that the whole matter of navigable waterways was given over by Congress to the Secretary of War and delegated by him to the Corps of Engineers. And what they said was that the recourse which anyone had, if he had any, in a situation such as that, was to the Corps of Engineers. And that unless and until the Corps acted on this matter, that there was nothing to come before the court. and it was with reference to that decision that the Court of Appeal in this case held that if that were a fact, if that fact were established, that then this would not be dispositive because it was first requisite that these respondents or these petitioners, I stand corrected, these petitioners should make application to the Corps of Engineers to declare that this was a waterway which had been obstructed. And I think it is quite clear under the Rivers and Harbors Act that it is the duty of the engineers to enforce the provisions of that act and where there has been any sort of impediment or any sort of action contrary to the provisions of the act, it is incumbent on the engineers to act. And that, I think, was the answer which the Court of Appeal of Louisiana gave. Is that responsive to your honor's question? Yes, it is. Let me say that I mention the other aspect of it because I think it is desirable, that is, the insufficiency of the affidavit, because I think it is desirable for this court to understand that no real issue of fact has been created by this affidavit under our Louisiana procedure. But I think the substantial answer is that which lies in the holding of the Court of Louisiana in Ilheny against Broussard. Now, if I may, Your Honor, let me say that I think the critical question and the critical area of inquiry in this case is, what are we talking about when we're talking about navigable bodies of water? It is our contention that the power of Congress under the Commerce Clause over navigable waters is one thing. The navigation servitude is quite enough. The navigation servitude... But you're separating the Rivers and Harbors Act, for example, from the other questions. Is that part of it? Well, the Rivers and Harbors Act... Pollution control, for example. Impediments to navigation. We are separating them in this sense, Mr. Chief Justice, which is that as we appreciate it, Congress' power to enact the Rivers and Harbors Act stems from the Commerce Clause. And it is in the exercise of its power under the Commerce Clause that it does legislate with respect to pollution, to flood control, to recreation, to those matters on which Congress has legislated. But what we say, and we believe that this is central to the whole controversy, is that the so-called servitude of navigation is only one aspect of Congress' power over navigable waters generally. So coming back to a question which was addressed by one of your honors to counsel, what is a navigable water? We would suggest to your honors that the answer to that depends on what your inquiry is. Because if you're talking about the servitude of navigation, that is one thing. If you're talking about say flood control, or if you're talking about something like that, it is another. Now, what is the... If you're talking about navigational servitude, that has nothing to do with Congressional action. And the second query is, if you're talking about Congressional power under the Commerce Clause, isn't that what you mean? Precisely, Your Honor. When I say, however, that it has nothing to do with it, I would accept counsel's statement that Congress power through the Commerce Clause over navigation, as it were, protect the servitude of navigation. But there exists a servitude with or without Congressional action. Precisely. And that servitude is fairly precisely defined in the number of decisions of this Court. And we were told in the earlier case that this stems from the common law of England adopted by the colonies of the United States sent carried forward as a matter of national impact in the Commerce Clause of our Constitution. But it has nothing to do with Congressional power under the Commerce Clause. Isn't that correct? Precisely. That is our point and that we believe that that is important to the resolution of the issues raised in this case. Now, the servitude of navigation is not coextensive with Congress power over commerce. It is limited. And the servitude of navigation is with relation to streams which are naturally navigable or as the phrase is sometimes used, in their normal or natural condition. Now, the distinction is important for this reason. That when Congress acts through its delegate, the Corps of Engineers, with respect to the area covered by the servitude of navigation, no compensation is necessary. And the reason for that is that the riparian owner has rights in that part of the stream which is covered, or the bank which is covered by the servitude of navigation, which is an imperfect right. He has a qualified title, and the qualification to that title is that the national power, Congress, may appropriate that portion of the stream which is subject to the servitude of navigation without any compensation whatsoever. Conversely, however, although there may be areas which are beyond the reach of the servitude of navigation, they may be appropriated by Congress in its exercise of its power over commerce, for example, flood control or something like that, but it must then pay just compensation. I think that possibly the best illustration of that is in the United States against Kansas City Life Company case. That was a case, your honors will recall, where there was a flood control or a dam which was constructed. And the consequence of that was that the water backed up. And the water backed up not only as to the banks of the river, that portion covered by the navigable servitude, but it backed up well beyond that onto fast land. And the holding of that case was that compensation was due to the extent that fast land was covered by the waters which it backed up. I think that one case, and there are several like that, illustrates possibly more clearly than any other the limits of the servitude of navigation. Now, coming back to this proposition that the servitude of navigation extends to waters in that natural and normal condition, it is true that this court and other courts has and have on occasion said that waters which may be in their normal or natural state are subject to reasonable improvement. But I would pose to your honors the question of how construction of a canal on what was formerly fast land could possibly be considered to be reasonable improvement. reasonable improvement of navigation, is that what you're saying? Of the stream itself or the navigability of the stream, yes, that is the point. Well, it's conceivable, isn't it, that you could have a navigable stream 20 feet wide and the Corps of Engineers would decide that it would be a better navigable stream, if it were 40 feet wide, and as a result they would have to take 10 feet of fast land off of each side of the stream. Now, in a case like that, I take it they would have to pay compensation. We would so contend, Your Honor, and we believe the cases so dictate. Now, the point of the navigation servitude is that if I, for example, have my grist mill on the back of that stream and the engineers take part of that stream and set it back so that I can't have my grist mill anymore, they must compensate me for my mill, but they don't have to compensate me for the fact that I can no longer use the power from that stream. And that, it seems to us, is one of the most critical aspects of this case. That what we're talking about here is, is there a servitude of navigation on these artificially constructed canals? The record is quite clear that these canals were all constructed on private land, by private individuals, with private funds. Mr. McCall, can I interrupt you for a second? In Mr. Justice Rehnquist's question about adding 20 feet to a canal or to a navigable stream, the extra 20 feet that were added would be navigable and would be subject to the servitude, would they not? It would, it would indeed. So your definition of naturally navigable waters wouldn't really be adequate to cover that extra 20 feet? That would come within reasonable improvement, as I appreciate it, your water. But then isn't the question here whether this is a reasonable improvement? Well, we take the position, and we believe that it's a sound one, that where you dig your canal from scratch, so to speak, that you're not reasonably improving the navigability of a stream. Of course, all these have always been hooked up to navigable waters, so they've just enlarged what started out as a lesser body of navigable water. No, sir. That's not correct, sir. These canals, there was nothing where these canals were before. If you will examine this plat, you will observe that the shape of these canals is such that it is quite clear that they were artificially created. They go in straight lines. They don't follow any sort of contour. Didn't they always hook up to some navigable, bayou, or canal? Otherwise, how will you've gotten the equipment into them? Well, yes, in the same way that my driveway and my country estate connects with a highway. Right. Because that's the whole purpose of it. Now, if I may call it, if you will, a digression, I would like to address the suggestion which is made by council that what we have done is that we have destroyed or impaired the usability of existing streams, which ties in a little bit with your question, Mr. Justice Stevens. And we would say as to that, that there is nothing in the record to support that contention. The deposition which is given by Mr. Donoghue, who was the manager of Respondent, is to the effect that the only stream which has only body of water or bayou which has been interfered with is former freshwater bayou which has been replaced by the canal which the Corps of Engineers constructed. And I would refer, your honors, to freshwater bayou canal, which is the wide canal coming from the gulf proceeding up. This photograph is oriented with north at the top. Goes up north and just at the juncture with the canal which goes off to the left, your honors will see this obviously natural waterway which was freshwater bayou. Now, freshwater bayou, as can be seen from that, is no longer usable, but not by reason of any canal constructed by the Respondent, but purely by construction of the Engineers Canal, freshwater bayou canal, to which, as I said in an earlier question, public access is given. But this gets back to the Louisiana Court of Appeals statement that the, at least the defense claimed, whether factually, correctly, or otherwise, that your system of artificial waterways destroyed the navigability of surrounding natural waterways. waterways. And they didn't reject that as a thing, it's factually untrue. They said whether factually true or not, it doesn't make any difference under Louisiana law. But I must confess that that is correct. Or under federal law. They did say, they did say that. But my point is that had they chosen to have done so, they could have gone further and said that there is not a sufficient factual issue here to present this to us for disposition. What they said instead was that pre-demitting the question of whether there is such an issue, it would not make any difference as a matter of law. Right. Precisely as your honor has said. Even if the defendants are correct about that. Even if the petitioners in this case are correct, that's what the court will feel said. Yes, that's correct, your honor. They do say that. It's nonetheless the same. That's what the opinion reads. Right. But as I say, we say that beyond that, that there is no such issue and that whereas this is what the court said, that the court could just as well have said, there is no such issue. Yeah, but it didn't. Quite right. And I won't labor that point because I think that's quite clear, that they did not say that.
